Look, I've read both the aggressive and conservative cases carefully, and I think both of them are making the same category of error — each is taking one true feature of the A-share market and extrapolating it into a thesis that the other features don't support. Let me be specific about where each one overreaches before I lay out what I think the balanced answer actually is.

The aggressive analyst's core claim is that this is a left-side entry at an emotional extreme, and that the four cushions — valuation, zero lockup, policy put, sentiment — make 1426 a high-odds add. The problem isn't that the individual observations are wrong. RSI 21 is genuine, the band-break and 200-day loss are real, the supply report is genuinely clean. The problem is the inference structure. He takes a condition (oversold, extreme, cheap-relative-to-history) and treats it as a signal (bottom is in). Those aren't the same thing, and the technical report is unusually explicit about it — RSI is still falling, no inflection, no bullish divergence, MACD accelerating below zero. He says the RSI base rate of double-digit bounces after 22 is the argument. But he's selecting the base rate conditionally on the outcome he wants. The honest base rate is: extreme oversold raises the probability of a bounce at *some* point over the next weeks, and says almost nothing about whether today's 1426 holds. His tranche plan — 1426, 1390-1400, 1350 — actually concedes this, because he expects it can go another 5%+ down. So he isn't really calling a bottom. He's averaging into a falling knife with a plan that works only if the gaps are small and the stops are executable.

And that's where the conservative analyst lands his strongest blow, and I think it's decisive against the aggressive position: T+1 plus an empty limit-down order book means the "ATR 35-45 yuan stop" is not a stop, it's a hope. The aggressive analyst's T+1-as-a-help argument — that it locks selling pressure and enables squeezes — is a real feature on the upside and a catastrophic feature on the downside, and the asymmetry matters because you can't hedge the overnight gap on a name with a 1.64 trillion market cap and a policy headline risk that arrives at 2am. That's a genuine structural point, not a US-market reflex.

But now let me turn on the conservative analyst, because he overcorrects in a way that's equally unsupported. His conclusion is "reduce to a gap-tolerant core, trim into strength above 1450-1485, cut further if 1425 fails." That's not crazy, but it makes two mistakes. First, he treats the neutral HOLD as if it were a decision to own full exposure through a distribution phase — but that's exactly what the trader's reasoning already guards against. The trader said explicitly: maintain a base position, don't clear out, don't short, don't left-side add, size so an overnight gap is survivable, and trim in tranches if the reduction triggers fire. That *is* the gap-tolerant core, already. The conservative analyst is arguing to do less of what the trader is already doing. Second, he treats the missing data as if it were a negative. He's right that the aggressive analyst is asymmetric to treat an unverified stimulus as a real +6-8% and an unverified tax as a footnote — that's a fair hit. But the conservative does the mirror image: he treats the absent batch-price and policy text as if it tilted bearish. It doesn't. Missing data is a reason to keep the position small and wait, not a reason to reduce it. He's using uncertainty to justify a directional action, which is the same error he's accusing the aggressive of making.

And the supply cushion — he's right that zero lockup expiry removes one source of new supply and is not a demand catalyst, and it's fair to call out that the aggressive analyst dresses the absence of a negative as a positive. But the conservative then underweights it in the other direction: a clean supply picture, a 14% leverage ratio, a 1.07 cash-to-earnings ratio and a 92% gross margin do tell you the *permanent capital impairment* risk is low. That doesn't tell you the price won't fall another 15%, and he's right to say so — but it does tell you that a moderate position held through this phase is not a reckless bet on a broken business. It's a bet that a fortress-balance-sheet asset at the low end of its own valuation band, with no new supply and a state shareholder that doesn't sell, will be worth more in twelve months than today. That's a reasonable bet to hold at moderate size. It's not a reasonable bet to size up into.

So here's where I come out, and I want to be precise because the framing of this whole conversation keeps collapsing into "add" versus "cut."

The aggressive analyst is right that RSI 21 on a 92%-gross-margin, 37%-ROE, zero-debt business with no lockup and a state anchor at the low end of its historical PE band is a bad place to be short or flat with zero exposure. He's wrong to call it an add window, because the technical structure is still accelerating down, the value cushion he cites has a further 15-25% of multiple-compression room on the fundamentals report's own numbers, and his exit discipline doesn't execute in the tail. The correct conclusion from his own data is: don't be short, don't be flat, but don't press.

The conservative analyst is right that the T+1 gap tail is unhedgeable and that the data vacuum argues for caution. He's wrong to translate that into reducing a position that's already been sized for survivability, and wrong to treat information absence as a bearish signal. The trader isn't carrying unhedged full exposure — the trader is carrying a base position with explicit tranche-reduction triggers and a stated preference for right-side confirmation before upgrading. That's already the conservative posture he's asking for.

The balanced answer is the one the trader actually wrote, and I'd defend it but sharpen the sizing logic. Hold the base. Don't add at 1426 — the MACD is still widening, the close was at the day's low, VWMA confirms distribution, and there's no divergence. Don't cut into the hole either — the supply side is genuinely clean, the balance sheet makes permanent impairment unlikely, and the name is at the low end of its own valuation band, so a full exit at an emotional extreme with no confirming negative catalyst beyond price is selling certainty cheaply. Size the core so that a limit-down overnight gap is annoying but not portfolio-impairing — that's the honest translation of "T+1 is a double-edged sword": you don't get to claim the squeeze upside without accepting the gap downside, so you size for the gap and let the squeeze be a bonus. Set the trim triggers where the trader did — if 1425 fails on volume, reduce in tranches; if it reclaims 1450-1485 with volume contraction, you have the right-side confirmation to consider upgrading. And critically, don't upgrade the position on the strength of the policy put until you have the actual text of the consumption tax and stimulus documents, because the policy report is honest that it verified nothing — and the aggressive analyst's probability weighting is doing more work than the evidence permits.

The meta-point I'd make to both of them: the aggressive analyst is pricing the option as if it's free and the gap is small. The conservative analyst is pricing the position as if the gap is large and the option is worthless. The A-share structure says both are true at different times, and the only way to survive both is to hold a moderate, tranche-managed core and let the market tell you which regime you're in before you commit more capital. That's not splitting the difference for its own sake. It's the only position whose downside is defined and whose upside isn't surrendered — which is exactly what T+1, limit-down order books, and a policy calendar you can't verify actually require of you.

So: HOLD, at a size you can survive gapping, with the trader's reduction triggers live and a hard rule against adding until either the right-side technical confirmation or the actual policy text arrives. Not because I'm afraid of the tail and not because I want to catch the bounce — but because that's the only construction where the aggressive analyst's upside and the conservative analyst's capital protection aren't mutually exclusive.
